query: Which mixed-effects model specifications (random intercepts/slopes, nesting by course/instructor) best control for discipline and L1 when analysing disclosure and quality outcomes?

response.query: Which mixed-effects model specifications (random intercepts/slopes, nesting by course/instructor) best control for discipline and L1 when analysing disclosure and quality outcomes?
response.answer: For disclosure and quality outcomes, use random intercepts for course and instructor, and random slopes for discipline and L1. This controls for individual and group-level variability.

This model would have four fixed-effect parameters and (4\*(4+1)/2)=10 covariance parameters for each random effect. On the other hand, if (say) difficulty and consistency are properties of items (so that, say, item 23 is always in difficulty class 'hard' and 'consistent'), then you would only use `(1 | Item)`. if `a` is a categorical variable with levels `A` and `B`, `1 + a` expands to a two-column model matrix with columns `(Intercept)` and `B` (== indicator variable for group B), while `0 + a` *still expands to a 2-column model matrix*, this time with columns `A` and `B` (both indicator variables). Bring the best of human thought and AI automation together at your work. # How to specify random slopes when random effects are nested or crossed. I'm trying to run a model which has 3 random effects. Its data on an animal species and the random effects are 'group', 'mother' and 'individual'. Individual should be nested within mother, and then both are crossed within group separately, because both individuals and their mother can move to different groups independent from one another. (1|group:mother/individual) - does this account for the fact that an individual could move to another group, without its mother, or would they always have to be nested together? N.B. I'm using glmmTMB and also wasn't sure if it recognise the crossed/nested nature of the random effects without specifying them. Following on from this using a maximal random slopes framework, for 5 different fixed effects, I would like to specify different random slopes for each of the random effects. Is it possible to specify different random slopes for the different random effects when they are already denoted as crossed or nested? If I cannot pick different nest/crossed random effects should the different random slopes take priority or the nesting/crossing of the random effects? ## 1 Answer 1. Question 1 is a quick no. Individual nested in mother and both crossed with group should be something like `(1|mother/individual) + (1|group)`. `(1|mother/individual) + (1|group)`. For question 2, the crossed random effects definitely don't care for the nested on we can use the alternative notation `(1|mother/individual) = (1|mother)+(1|mother:individual)`, now replace the 1s with what you want. `(1|mother/individual) = (1|mother)+(1|mother:individual)`. Question 3 shouldn't be an issue, however with many random effects/slopes, many of them correlated you will likely get a singular fit, i.e. the variation of the random effects is 0 in some "direction". Thanks for contributing an answer to Cross Validated! Find the answer to your question by asking.

Title: regression - Random Effects Model Suitable for Analysing Survey Data? - Cross Validated

Stack Overflow for Teams is now called **Stack Internal**. Bring the best of human thought and AI automation together at your work. # Random Effects Model Suitable for Analysing Survey Data? I have a large survey dataset covering 13 countries and am interested in finding out how each respondent's index score differs according to their age, gender and marriage status. I would like to know if their score differs as a function of these variables. Would a random effects model be suitable for this purpose? ## 1 Answer 1. A model with random effects, ie a mixed effects model is useful when you have clustering of observations. This is because responses will be more similar within the same cluster than other clusters - that is, they will not be independent. Random effects are also useful when you are not interested in the systematic effect of a grouping variable. You mention Countries, so that is one level of clustering. Mixed effects models are also useful when you have nesting, for example if your data also includes cities then cities would be nested in countries. This type of model is sometimes called a multilevel model, but it is just a special case of a mixed effects model. So yes, it would seem that a model with random intercepts for countries could be appropriate here. `index ~ age + sex + marriage + (age + sex + marriage | countryID)`. ## Your Answer.
